subject: Fysik
title: Electricity and circuits
sourceSummary: Voltage, current and resistance with the correct units, Ohm's law at a basic level, and the difference between series and parallel circuits. This also covers circuit diagrams, fuses and electrical safety.

questions.prompt: In which unit is voltage measured?
questions.opener: Each electrical quantity has its own unit — think about what's printed on a battery.
choices: Ampere (A)
Volt (V)
Ohm (Ω)
Watt (W)
questions.explanation: Voltage (U) is measured in volts (V) — that's why a battery is labelled, for example, 1.5 V. Ampere is the unit for current, ohm for resistance and watt for power.

questions.prompt: A current of 2 A flows through a resistor of 5 Ω. What is the voltage across the resistor according to Ohm's law (U = R · I)?
questions.opener: Here both the resistance and the current are known, so you can use the formula exactly as it stands.
choices: 7 V
questions.explanation: U = R · I = 5 Ω · 2 A = 10 V. Dividing 5 by 2 instead gives 2.5, and adding the numbers gives 7 — both are common mistakes when you lose track of which quantity you're solving for.

questions.prompt: Two resistors of 3 Ω and 4 Ω are connected in series. What happens to the total resistance?
questions.opener: In a series circuit, the current must pass through both resistors one after the other.
choices: It becomes the sum, 7 Ω — that is, greater than either of the resistors
It becomes 1 Ω, that is, the difference between the resistors
It becomes 12 Ω, that is, the product of the resistors
It becomes less than 3 Ω
questions.explanation: In a series circuit, resistances are added: R = 3 Ω + 4 Ω = 7 Ω. The total resistance is always greater than the largest single resistor. The total resistance becoming less than the smallest resistor applies to a parallel circuit, not a series circuit.

questions.prompt: Three lamps are connected in parallel to a 6 V battery. What voltage is across each lamp?
questions.opener: In a parallel circuit, each lamp sits directly between the battery's two terminals.
choices: 2 V, the voltage is shared equally between the lamps
18 V, the voltage is added for each lamp
6 V, each lamp gets the full battery voltage
It's impossible to know without knowing the resistance
questions.explanation: In a parallel circuit, the same voltage, 6 V, is across every branch. It is in a series circuit that the voltage is divided between the components — that's why lamps in parallel shine just as brightly as if they were connected alone.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that the circuit is closed in a circuit diagram?
questions.opener: Look at whether the current has an unbroken path all the way around.
choices: That the switch is open so nothing can happen
That there is an unbroken conducting path from one terminal of the battery through the components back to the other terminal
That the circuit only contains a single component
That all the components are drawn with the same symbol
questions.explanation: A closed circuit is an unbroken current path from one terminal of the battery, through the components, and back to the other terminal — only then can current flow. An open switch instead breaks the circuit, and then the lamp goes out.

questions.prompt: What is the job of a fuse in an electrical installation?
questions.opener: Think about what would happen to the wires if far too much current flowed through them.
choices: It increases the voltage in the circuit so the appliances work better
It measures how much electricity you use
It makes sure the current always flows in the same direction
It cuts the current if the current strength becomes too high, so the wires don't overheat and catch fire
questions.explanation: A fuse is a deliberate weak point that trips and breaks the circuit when the current becomes dangerously high, for example during a short circuit or an overload. It doesn't measure electricity consumption — the electricity meter does that — and it doesn't affect the voltage.

questions.prompt: A current of 0.5 A flows through a small motor when it is connected to a voltage of 6 V. Calculate the motor's resistance.
questions.opener: Ohm's law is U = R · I. Rearrange for R before you plug in the values.
steps: Write down what you know: U = 6 V and I = 0.5 A.
Start from Ohm's law: U = R · I.
Rearrange for the resistance: R = U / I.
Plug in the values: R = 6 V / 0.5 A.
Dividing by 0.5 is the same as multiplying by 2, so R = 12 Ω.

questions.prompt: Summarise the electrical quantities with their units, Ohm's law, series and parallel circuits, and electrical safety.
questions.opener: Take one quantity at a time with the correct unit, link them together with Ohm's law, and finish with the types of connection.
questions.answer: Voltage (U), volt (V): the driving force that makes the charges move · Current (I), ampere (A): how much charge passes per second · Resistance (R), ohm (Ω): the opposition that slows the current · Ohm's law: U = R · I, so I = U/R and R = U/I · Closed circuit: an unbroken current path from one terminal of the battery back to the other — otherwise no current flows · Series circuit: a single current path, resistances are added, the same current everywhere, the voltage is divided up, one break switches everything off · Parallel circuit: several branches, the same voltage across each branch, the current is divided up, a break in one branch doesn't affect the others — used in houses · Circuit diagram: a circuit drawn with standard symbols for a battery, lamp, switch and resistor · Fuse: breaks the circuit at too high a current, protects against overheating and fire · Electrical safety: a short circuit gives a very high current, a residual-current device (RCD) trips quickly on a fault, only experiment with low voltages.
